title: Linear Optimization I: The Art of Formulation
subtitle: Decision variables, objectives, and constraints — the three-part grammar that turns messy business problems into solvable models

objectives.title: Translate business problems into LP form
objectives.description: Identify decision variables, write a linear objective, and express real constraints — capacity, demand, quality specs — as linear inequalities.

objectives.title: Read the geometry of an LP
objectives.description: Explain the feasible region, why optimal solutions live at corner points, and what binding vs. non-binding constraints mean for a manager.

objectives.title: Build and solve your first gurobipy model
objectives.description: Set up a free Gurobi academic license, write a production-mix model in Google Colab, and interpret the solver output line by line.

objectives.title: Recognize LP structure in the wild
objectives.description: See how production mix and blending problems share one skeleton — and why that skeleton powers everything from refineries to Google's data centers.

agenda.title: Story Hook: Google's Carbon-Aware Compute
agenda.description: A 2026 Franz Edelman Award finalist, Google shifts massive data-center workloads across time and geography to chase clean electricity — and the engine under the hood is linear programming. We reverse-engineer the decision: what are they choosing, what are they maximizing, what limits them?
bulletPoints: Compute jobs move to hours and regions where the grid is greenest
Every LP has the same three parts: decisions, objective, constraints
If a trillion-dollar company runs on LP, your spreadsheet problems definitely can

agenda.title: The Formulation Grammar
agenda.description: The single most valuable skill in this course: turning a paragraph of business prose into decision variables, an objective function, and constraints. We formulate a two-product production-mix problem live, from words to algebra.
bulletPoints: Decision variables: what is actually under your control?
Objective: one number you want biggest or smallest
Constraints: machine-hours, labor, demand ceilings, non-negativity
Common trap: modeling outcomes instead of decisions

agenda.title: LP Geometry: Why Corners Win
agenda.description: We graph the feasible region of our production-mix problem and slide the profit line until it leaves the polygon. The optimum always lands on a corner — that geometric fact is why LPs with millions of variables solve in seconds.
bulletPoints: Feasible region = every plan that breaks no rules
Corner points are where constraints intersect — and where optima live
Binding constraints touch the optimum; slack constraints have room to spare

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, and get your Gurobi academic license request submitted if you haven't already.

agenda.title: Hands-On Lab: First gurobipy Model in Colab
agenda.description: Laptops open. We activate the free academic license, then build the production-mix model in gurobipy from a blank Colab cell: variables, objective, constraints, optimize, and read the solution.
bulletPoints: License setup at gurobi.com/academics — free with your suffolk.edu email
addVar, setObjective, addConstr, optimize — the four verbs of gurobipy
Verify the solver's answer against the corner point we found graphically

agenda.title: Blending Problems: Same Skeleton, New Skin
agenda.description: From gasoline blending to animal feed to coffee roasting, blending problems are where LP earned its first industrial fortunes. We formulate a fuel-blending example with quality specs as ratio constraints — and learn the linearization trick that makes ratios legal.
bulletPoints: Blend ingredients to hit quality specs at minimum cost
Ratio constraints must be cross-multiplied into linear form
Refineries have run LP daily since the 1950s — billions saved per year industry-wide

agenda.description: Recap the formulation grammar, preview sensitivity analysis and shadow prices coming next week, and walk through the blending homework so everyone leaves knowing exactly what to build.
bulletPoints: Homework #1: formulate and solve a blending problem in gurobipy

activities.title: Production-Mix LP in gurobipy
activities.description: Build a furniture-maker's weekly production plan: two products competing for limited carpentry and finishing hours. Formulate on paper, then solve in Colab and confirm the answer sits on the corner point you predicted.

steps.title: Formulate on paper first
steps.description: Define x_desks and x_chairs, write the profit objective, and express carpentry and finishing capacity as linear constraints. No code until the algebra is done.

steps.title: Code the model in gurobipy
steps.description: Translate your formulation line-for-line: one addVar per decision, setObjective for profit, one addConstr per resource limit.

steps.title: Solve and interpret
steps.description: Run optimize(), read the optimal plan and profit, and check which constraints are binding (used to the last hour) versus slack.

steps.title: Stress-test the model
steps.description: Add a demand cap of 30 desks and re-solve. Watch how the optimal corner moves — your first taste of what-if analysis.

codeBlock.code:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

m = gp.Model("production_mix")

# Decision variables: units to produce this week
desks = m.addVar(name="desks")
chairs = m.addVar(name="chairs")

# Objective: maximize total profit ($)
m.setObjective(70 * desks + 50 * chairs, GRB.MAXIMIZE)

# Constraints: limited shop-floor hours
m.addConstr(4 * desks + 3 * chairs <= 240, "carpentry_hours")
m.addConstr(2 * desks + 1 * chairs <= 100, "finishing_hours")

m.optimize()

print(f"Build {desks.X:.0f} desks and {chairs.X:.0f} chairs")
print(f"Weekly profit: ${m.ObjVal:,.0f}")

activities.discussionNote: Both resource constraints are binding at the optimum — the shop uses every carpentry hour and every finishing hour. So which resource would you expand first if you could? You cannot answer that from the solution alone. Hold that thought: it is exactly the question shadow prices answer in Session 3.

takeaways.text: Every LP is three questions: What can I decide? What am I maximizing or minimizing? What rules can I not break? Master that grammar and you can model almost any resource-allocation problem.
Optimal solutions live at corner points of the feasible region — the geometric insight that lets solvers crush million-variable problems, from a furniture shop to Google's global data-center fleet.
Formulate on paper before you type. gurobipy is just a transcription tool — the model in your head is the real deliverable.

homework.label: Homework #1
homework.text: The Blending Challenge: a specialty coffee roaster blends three bean origins (each with a cost per pound, caffeine content, and flavor score) into a house blend that must hit minimum quality specs at minimum cost. Formulate the LP on paper (variables, objective, constraints), then solve it in gurobipy in Colab. Submit your Colab notebook plus a five-sentence plain-English summary of the optimal blend and total cost. Due before Session 3.
